speechtext:

subsubtopic: SETTLEMENT OF EAST COAST MARITIME BOUNDARY BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES-NEED FOR FISHERIES CONSERVATION AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans I will direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, simply because the questions overlap.
Yesterday an official of the United States state department stated that no negotiations on an east coast fisheries treaty between the United States and Canada will begin until the maritime boundary dispute between the two countries is settled by the International Court of Justice at the Hague, an action which I submit will take at least four or five years. Is it the intention of the present government to continue its conservation quotas for Canadians in this area until the boundary dispute is settled?
Will the government persecute the crews of nine scallop draggers, which were raided yesterday in my home town of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, for allegedly catching undersized scallops, when Americans catch and market the same size scallops, or will an attempt be made to secure an interim conservation agreement with the United States for the benefit of the fishermen of both countries?
Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Madam Speaker, I think I should leave it to my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, to answer part of that question on a subsequent occasion. But with respect to the international aspect of it, let me say that it is
very important to distinguish between a fisheries agreement, even an interim fisheries agreement, and a conservation plan.
As I understood the comment made yesterday before the United States Senate committee by a U.S. government official, he was talking about a full interim fisheries arrangement.
I think we would have to say that we sadly regard the fisheries arrangement in the form of a treaty as no longer possible of attainment until the boundary question is settled. But with respect to conservation measures, we stated very forcefully to the Americans last week, during their visit, that we not only expected to be fully consulted on a conservation measure which they would bring into force, but that we expected a conservation measure to be put into effect. Of course, that is also the position we would prefer to continue with our own fishermen.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADIAN DELEGATION VISIT WASHINGTON
REQUEST THAT CANADIAN DELEGATION VISIT WASHINGTON
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. In light of the position stated yesterday by an official of the United States state department before its Senate foreign relations committee that recall of the fisheries treaty is "total", and that no negotiations can begin, even on an interim solution, until the maritime boundary question is settled and, as I said a moment ago, in light of the present overfishing by Americans in this area and the potential for complete destruction of the stocks if this action continues indefinitely, will the minister take the initiative to put together a delegation led by himself, consisting of officials of his department, Members of Parliament from all parties who are interested, and fishing groups, to approach the United States government in an attempt to persuade it to modify its position on this important matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADIAN DELEGATION VISIT WASHINGTON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure we have to persuade the United States administration to modify its position, because it wants a conservation measure as much as we do. It may well be difficult to set it up with the co-operation of the fishermen of the United States.
Certainly I appreciate the fact that there is good will on all sides of the House with respect to this, and that we all have a common interest in putting forward a strong position vis-a-vis the United States government, particularly the United States Congress. I will certainly discuss with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans the hon. member's suggestion about the appropriate forms of representation, including a delegation.

subtopic: QUOTAS ALLOCATED TO EUROPEAN FISHING FLEETS
QUOTAS ALLOCATED TO EUROPEAN FISHING FLEETS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer. I can assure him that we are endeavouring to be helpful and will concur in any genuine effort which is made to try to come to some form of agreement.
March 19, 1981

Since we are obviously facing an impasse on fisheries problems between our two countries, has the minister considered discussing with his colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, revising the fishing quotas allocated to European-based fishing fleets within our 200-mile limit, and using those stocks as a bargaining chip to induce the American government to take a more enlightened position on the fisheries management treaty, since at present there is no quid pro quo for,Canada on these fishing quotas now being allocated to European-based fleets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: QUOTAS ALLOCATED TO EUROPEAN FISHING FLEETS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, with respect to any existing arrangements by which we are bound with European countries, I think we would not be at liberty to depart from those. In fact, we are in the process of negotiating a new arrangement with the European Economic Community. At the moment it seems that it will not be very easily negotiated. Perhaps in light of that fact there may be, indeed, additional fish and additional fishing quotas about which the hon. member and I could talk.

subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF WEST COAST FISHING BOUNDARY
NEGOTIATION OF WEST COAST FISHING BOUNDARY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. On March 9 in this House the Secretary of State undertook to raise west coast boundary and fisheries treaty matters on the occasion of the visit of the President of the United States. I would like to ask the minister if press reports are correct to the effect that Canada has reached a tentative agreement, not merely at the officials level but at the political level, on either the west coast fisheries salmon treaty or the boundaries issue? If not, what progress has been made in recent days as a consequence of the recent visit by the President of the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: NEGOTIATION OF WEST COAST FISHING BOUNDARY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there has been considerable progress made with respect to the tuna fishery on the west coast, but with respect to the salmon and boundaries questions, those are at an earlier stage.
However, our negotiators report that they have achieved significant advances in the talks. Therefore, in the near future cabinet will have to decide whether or not to go on with the negotiations and, of course, the terms on which the negotiations should continue.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE RECOMMENDATIONS
BRITISH COLUMBIA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to hear that. In the same vein, then, I would like to ask either the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, who has just taken his seat, or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, what specific boundaries on the west coast the government is prepared to advance on behalf of Canada? I ask this in light of recent submissions and resolutions passed
Oral Questions
by the British Columbia Chamber of Commerce which suggest that Canada stand firm on the traditional A-B boundary line in Dixon Entrance, insist on redrawing the fisheries boundary off the coast of the Alaska panhandle to reflect better the traditional fishing access of Canadian fishing vessels and, finally, that the federal government reflect the proposal of the provincial government that, in the San Juan extension, the southern fishery boundary follow the San Juan Canyon route rather than the equidistant line.
Will the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans or the Secretary of State tell the House if the Government of Canada will follow these recommendations of the B.C. Chamber of Commerce and British Columbia fishermen? If these matters cannot be resolved by bilateral discussion, may the House be informed as to whether they also could be submitted to the international tribunal, should that initiative be required with respect to east coast boundaries matters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA CHAMBER OF COMMERCE RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we will take very seriously the representations both of the hon. gentleman and of his province. I think I should distinguish between the two issues. On the salmon issue, the negotiations have made great progress and are far advanced. The boundaries issue is not at that stage at this time. As I said, we will very seriously consider this point of view.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT DOCTORS EXERCISE RESTRAINT IN FEE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Yesterday the minister offered voluntary restraint by organized labour, organized business and individuals as his flimsy solution to the problems of a 12.2 per cent inflation rate. Wage increases have fallen behind the cost of living for the fourth year in a row.
Since the doctors of Manitoba are demanding 49 per cent fee increases, B.C. doctors are demanding a 44 per cent hike, and the Ontario doctors just turned down a 15 per cent offer, does the minister intend to call in the heads of the provincial medical associations and ask the doctors of Canada to restrain their excessively inflationary demands before our medicare scheme is wrecked?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT DOCTORS EXERCISE RESTRAINT IN FEE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it would be more appropriate for provincial ministers to deal with the question of rising costs in provinces. As the hon. member may recall, the last time we had a very serious increase in wage rates in Canada the provincial premiers themselves met together and requested the federal government to take action in the way of wage and price controls. It seems to me that it would be appropriate, at an early stage, for all levels of government to

March 19, 1981
Oral Questions
take into account the impact of excessive wage settlements or wage demands in the current inflationary environment. 1 appreciate the interest of the hon. member in drawing this very important matter to our attention.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT OIL COMPANIES FREEZE PRICES TEMPORARILY
REQUEST THAT OIL COMPANIES FREEZE PRICES TEMPORARILY
speechtext:
Passing the buck to the provincial ministers may be all well and good, but in this case let us examine the oil companies, those dandy corporate citizens, whose profits are up 40 per cent over the last year, and just got caught with their arm in the cookie jar for another $12 billion; $175 million on inventory mark-ups-a big cookie jar-with six cents a gallon on oil, piggybacked on the March 1 price increase.
I would like the minister to call in those oil maggots, just for a little friendly discussion, and examine with them the effect of their behaviour on inflation rates in Canada, and to ask these high rollers to set an example for the rest of the country by freezing the price of oil, at least for a while.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT OIL COMPANIES FREEZE PRICES TEMPORARILY
speechtext:
All along, the government has resisted the requests of the oil industry to move up oil prices to the world level. We have taken quite a different view in that respect than the industry itself because we understand the impact which accelerating energy prices does have and is having, and which, if moved to the world level, would be even greater. For example, in the last year energy prices increased 24 per cent. We believe that is considerable. I want to assure the hon. member that that particular point has been taken into account.
In addition to that, I remind him that in the budget I did levy additional taxes on the oil and gas industry. In all honesty, I am somewhat disappointed by the lack of enthusiasm of the New Democratic Party for these additional taxes on the oil and gas industry.
The minister, in his obfuscation, neglected to mention the profits and the excessive gouging. That is really what my question was about. Let us take the chartered banks. We have here-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Would the hon. member just ask the question?
Just ask the question, Madam Speaker said. You are not Ed Broadbent.

I want to ask whether the minister will call into his office the heads of the chartered banks, who have similarly been profiteering, to talk to them about the spread between the interest rates on money which is on deposit and the interest rates which they charge for mortgages and loans. If the minister cannot bring the chartered banks into his office and
ask them for help, will he take a stroll down to the Senate where all the board members of the chartered banks sit?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: A stroll to the Senate seems more inviting than to call in the presidents of the banks. But let me-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Let me tell the hon. member that it is true that the profitability of the banks, as has been discussed in the House already, has been somewhat healthy in the last period. I have asked the House to take a look at the profitability of the banks over the preceding several quarters and over the preceding year to see whether, on the basis of a fairly extended period of time, a claim can be made that profits are excessive. It is for that reason that I have asked the House to take a longer view, not only of the past period but the current period and some months into the future, and at that time make up its mind whether, in fact, there have been excessive profits. In the meantime I intend to monitor the situation, and if action is required I will be prepared to consider it.

subtopic: PROTECTION FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AGAINST INFLATION
PROTECTION FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also addressed to the Minister of Finance who yesterday told this House that the Economic Council of Canada concurred with his view that Canada's old age pensioners are "fully protected" from inflation by the present system of indexing. Since the Economic Council of Canada said no such thing in its report on pensions, and since some preliminary estimates by former council staff indicate that pensioners are being short-changed by about $50 million to $60 million per year, will the minister either stop the sham of insisting that pensioners are being protected through indexing, or will he put some truth into the statement by returning that $50 million to $60 million to Canada's senior citizens?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROTECTION FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext: I disagree totally with the premise of the hon. member's question. I disagree totally and completely because the Canadian pension system-the guaranteed income supplement, the old age security-both systems, are fully guaranteed and adjusted quarterly, not bi-annually as suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

subtopic: PENSION PRICE INDEX FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
PENSION PRICE INDEX FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to see that the minister has such an open mind on this subject. I should like to point out to him that the estimated spread between the cost of living index and a pension price index is in the order of 4 per cent, which means that pensioners
March 19, 1981

today are facing 16 per cent inflation rather than the 12.2 per cent that has been indicated.
Will the minister at least re-examine an indexing system which pays pensions according to data which is seven years out of date and which does not reflect the spending habits of senior citizens or will he use his considerable influence in the government to ensure that necessary studies on a pension price index will take place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: PENSION PRICE INDEX FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I appreciate the constructive tone of the question and the constructive intention. speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: CANADIAN PLANS TO HELP EL SALVADORAN REFUGEES
speechtext:
As members of this House will recognize, Madam Speaker, the civil strife has caused a serious disruption and there are now an estimated 50,000 to 60,000 refugees on the border of El Salvador. I asked the officials to investigate the situation and work with the United Nations.
The United Nations High Commissioner has requested that there be no major movement of refugees at the present time. In the meantime, we are undertaking certain special measures such as those relating to Salvadorians in Canada now on business permits. They will be landed here if they are sponsored by relatives, or will be given minister's permits to provide for employment while they are here. After six months we will review their case with a view toward landing them. As well, those in Canada can sponsor relatives who have had to flee El Salvador because of reasons of strife. Those are intermediate measures. We will continue to monitor the situation and provide whatever relief this country can, within the tradition that we have already established.
