All these things I have enumerated manifest themselves daily. If we line up for a movie we will notice that Canadians stand patiently and are friendly in the line. We do not see Canadians barging in and trying to get to the front of the line. In other countries when there is a lineup for an event, people will try to break in and get to the front. There is a certain fairness that runs through the Canadian character. If hon. members will remember the last time they went into a grocery store or a drugstore and waited in a line-up to be served, and perhaps the clerk came forward and offered to take someone out of turn, the person addressed likely said that someone else was there before him. That is what makes the Canadian character; that is something fundamental that runs through it, the sense of fairness. Every night I give thanks to God for that sense of fairness in the Canadian mentality.
How has this developed? It is my contention it developed because of the many and varied ethnic groups who came to our shores and became Canadians while, at the same time, they retained their culture. We see evidence of it every day in various activities and languages. They became Canadian but maintained their heritage and their culture.
Had we moved into this constitutional debate in the true and typical Canadian manner, we would be celebrating the participation of all our people from coast to coast in the repatriation of our Constitution. We would be negotiating, compromising, working out solutions as reasonable men and women, because the ingrained fairness of the Canadian mentality would have prevailed.
Another example of the fairness and moderation of the Canadian mentality is seen daily in this House of Commons during question period when the cut and thrust of debate and the heckling goes on. But no member may rise in his place and use unparliamentary language. Even though one member may have written proof that another has lied, he may not call the other a liar or he will be named, because that is not parliamentary. I have great pride in being a Canadian because I see this fairness and tolerance demonstrated every day.
In the book "A Guide to the Peaceable Kingdom" Douglas Le Pan, poet and essayist, in an essay entitled "In Frock Coat and Moccasins" wrote:
Nor is it very difficult to understand why a Canadian passport should be so popular. Part of the explanation is that with it one can travel easily almost anywhere. Another reason for the popularity of the little blue booklet stamped in gold is that one can speak English or French or Ukrainian or Polish or Chinese and still be a Canadian. One can, in fact, be almost anyone and still be a Canadian; and to be a Canadian is to have a passport to the whole world.
Hear, hear!

When I read that, I get a lump in my throat. I have great pride in that statement. We should be focusing on that. This diversity is an advantage Canada has that no other country in the world enjoys.
A Toronto writer, Arnold Edinborough, said some time ago, "Canada has never been a melting pot; more like a tossed salad."
With respect to the resolution before this House of Commons, can any thinking man truly say that the Victoria charter amending formula proposed is fair to all Canadians when it makes central Canada senior or first-class provinces? The residents of central Canada become senior or first-class citizens, but in the hinterland provinces in the west and in the east, they become second-class citizens. They are second-class provinces, so it follows they are second-class citizens. That is not the Canadian way. That is not the Canadian mentality. That is not the fairness, the moderation, the co-operation or the tolerance of Canadians. That is not the Canadian way of doing things. It is as simple as that. It is absolutely unfair.
In section 46 we find the referendum proposal. The federal government can trigger and control a referendum which will pit region against region and Canadian against Canadian. This is not for a moment in keeping with the tradition of fairness and moderation. Minorities always suffer as a result of a referendum. It is absolutely unfair.
In Sections 36 to 44 we find the interim amending formula. It gives us the illusion that the government is prepared to be flexible when it is actually building toward the referendum option. That is not in the Canadian tradition. That is not moderation nor co-operation. Where is the fairness in that?
The government refuses to include a preamble to the Constitution, covering the principles which form the bases on which Canadians have lived, have been born, under which immigrants have entered the country, have built their homes and have become Canadians. These principles acknowledge the supremacy of God in every religion. These principles acknowledge there is a supreme architect of the universe. These principles acknowledge the dignity and rights of the human being, the equality of the sexes, the very importance of the family unit and the fundamental right to own property.
I have a letter which I think is most apt. In part, this letter, written to me, reads:
The individual who does not have the right to own property becomes, himself, the property of the state.
That is fundamental. It is not the Canadian way to exclude the right to own property. It is not the just way, nor can that be described as co-operation. I submit that if every Canadian were asked if they wanted those things I have mentioned included in the Constitution there would be a resounding yes from coast to coast. People want those principles recognized in any Constitution, not excluded.
I would now like to direct hon. members' attention to the resolution, including the charter of rights. I believe this resolution has been drafted in haste. I am positive there are members besides myself who have not made up their minds about the propriety of a charter of rights as a safeguard to human freedoms which are already upheld and protected in our existing common law, in our statutes, in our legal decisions, the current BN A Act, the Magna Carta and the Statutes of Westminster. significance to our whole way of life of an entrenched charter of rights. There are arguments equally valid on either side. I cannot go on the record in this House of Commons at this time stating which would be the best. There are equally valid arguments on both sides. Forcing this Constitution through so it will be approved by Great Britain is not fair to the Canadian tradition. It negates all of the qualities I have been talking about which make up that Canadian character.
Is this fetish to entrench the charter of rights by the present Prime Minister truly a recognition of a need in Canada? I cannot remember a great hue and cry from across this country that people feared for their rights and were being treated unjustly or that their rights were in danger. Is there an underlying motive which the Prime Minister has in insisting on entrenchment? 1 submit to this chamber that there is an underlying motive. The Prime Minister of Canada is attempting to entrench language equality in the Canadian Constitution in such a way that future generations of Canadians will never be able to alter.
On page 37 of Hansard for October 12, 1978, the Prime Minister, referring to the Constitution, is reported as saying:
It is vital to me that it does give protection to the kind of linguistic equality that this government has put into the statutes.
In other words, over two and a half years ago, the Prime Minister stated his very clear objective that he was going to entrench forever the concept of a Canada with two official languages. At least the Official Languages Act can be amended. This ability to amend gave the Canadian people the flexibility to change as the demography of our country changes, as it grows and progresses. But more important, it allows our children and our children's children if the need arises to change it 100 or 200 years from now when members of this House are nothing but a bad memory. The Prime Minister's objective is to protect his official language concept for all time. It is not fair. It is not fair to the people of Quebec either. It is not the Canadian way.
At the constitutional conference in September, 1980, Quebec firmly opposed the entrenchment of language rights. In its paper we read that the "very act of entrenching rights in the Constitution would freeze them for future generations." I submit to members of this House of Commons that the flexibility which has been so necessary for Canada to develop to the strong proud nation it is today will be gone forever.
Quebec's Bill 101 was very controversial but I did not hear a great hue and cry in my province that Bill 101 would destroy Canada because it declared that the business language in Quebec would be French. Why was Quebec allowed to pass that bill? I suggest it is because of the Canadian character to recognize, moderate and co-operate with French-speaking Canadians in Quebec who are a very strong majority in that province. Therefore, they have the right to insist that within their borders the language for business and institutions will be French. There was some flare-up, a little here and there. Some people discussed it and it was reported in the papers. However,
The Constitution
in the end the Canadian character, fairness and justice prevailed. Canadians from coast to coast recognized that those in Quebec must protect the French language or it will die, because they are surrounded throughout the North American continent by English-speaking people.
The people of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Newfoundland are being forced in exactly the same way. We are undermining the province of Quebec by forcing equality of the English language in that province just as we are causing an injustice to the people of British Columbia and in other non-French-speaking areas by forcing the French language on them.
We are attempting to force entrenchment of the English language on Quebec. It will destroy that province. The Quebec government recognizes that French is a regional language. Statistics Canada confirms that. There is a small minority of French-speaking people in provinces other than Quebec and New Brunswick; l'/2 per cent of the population in British Columbia and one-half of one per cent in Newfoundland.
It would be far better to allow the French language to flourish within Quebec and allow Bill 101 to stand. At the same time, those who desire can speak English. We must recognize that English is the unifying language of this country from Newfoundland to British Columbia. That does not show disrespect for the French language or for the rights of Frenchspeaking people in Canada.
It is not in the Canadian personality to force two official languages on Canadians. Every reference to the two equal languages causes disunity in this country. There are two versions of the Constitution in two official languages. The Prime Minister says they have equal authority. Imagine all the problems of trying to decipher and compare the two.
Canada will be the only country in the world with two separate Constitutions. I find that unbelievable. We will build two countries with two differing peoples. We are dividing this country as sure as I am standing here. We will have two separate identities for all time, and that is not the Canadian way. We will be entrenching hyphenated Canadianism, the French-speaking Canadian with his Constitution and the English-speaking Canadian with his. We will be building into the Constitution a sense of division that hearkens back to the original struggle. Language was not the thing that made us Canadian. We must heed the clarion call of John Diefenbaker and eradicate hyphenated Canadianism. I quote from volume one of John Diefenbaker's memoires:
I have always considered the official policy of separating our country into various racial groups to be a curse on the realization of a united Canada. One Canada, one nation, my Canada, your Canada, cannot be a hyphenated Canada.
If we want confirmation of this fact from another world statesman, let us look at the words of President Harry Truman, as they appeared in People magazine on February 16 of this year. These words came from his private papers. He said:
I've no more use for Polish-Americans, Irish-Americans, Swedish-Americans or any other sort of hyphenate than I have for Communist-Americans. They all have some other loyalty than the one they should have.

March 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
One of the lasting curses on the unity of this nation has been the terminology of the B and B Commission that gave us "anglophone" and "francophone". The two terms attempt to define what is a Canadian, and that is wrong. Those words should be stricken from the Canadian vocabulary.
Prior to patriation, I urge that we sit down with the provinces in a Canadian, moderate, co-operative, tolerant way, work out an amending formula and then bring the Constitution home. Then in a reasonable way we can amend our Constitution as the need arises and the people of Canada could express their opinions. I plead with hon. members not to accept the dictatorial proposal of the Prime Minister and the Liberal government.
In conclusion, I want to quote from an open letter to the Prime Minister on the constitutional debate from J. Borowski. I quote:
It is one thing to disregard the wishes, opinions or suggestions of your political opposition, but it is quite another matter when you arrogantly ignore the honestly and sincerely held views of a majority of your fellow Canadians.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise in my place to take part in the debate on this resolution and the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp). May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-TERMINATION OF NATIVE SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM
FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-TERMINATION OF NATIVE SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I take the opportunity to congratulate Premier Bill Davis on his delightful victory in today's Ontario provincial election.

subtopic: FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-TERMINATION OF NATIVE SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-TERMINATION OF NATIVE SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
This may be a lesson for the Liberal government which does not take its role towards native people programs very seriously, and that is exactly what I am going to talk about today. I refer to a question on February 13, page 7215 of Hansard.
The whole issue of programs for our native peoples, in my opinion, is one which requires immediate and serious consideration. It is time to stop shunting them from one department to
another with programs that attempt to solve problems only after they occur.
In this particular instance, the cancellation of the Indian sport and recreation program by the Department of Fitness and Amateur Sport, and the transfer of funds which were allocated for this program in the estimates to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, is a classic example of insensitivity and the lack of foresight on the part of this government in dealing with the people of this country. As I understand it, the money will now be used for health care programs. Whatever happened to the premise that "an ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure"?
How long will it take the government to realize that sport and recreation programs are essential to the well-being of all Canadians, and this includes our native people? This government, which is willing at great expense to find out statistically how badly we as Canadians measure up in fitness tests, is not willing to fund the kind of programs which will improve this level of fitness. We might as well have had a royal commission, for all the good the results of the fitness tests will do us.
With the soaring costs of medical care, why can the government not see how much more logical it would be to fund programs which would improve the physical fitness of individuals, and thus reduce the need for medical care? This is not a new theory. The government has no need to check out the equation that fitness equals health. This has been done repeatedly by many qualified individuals and groups, and has been accepted by all.
The private sector is beginning to move in the direction of offering fitness programs for employees. The benefits of course are obvious; less absence from work, higher production levels and better working relations between individuals. These benefits, though not directly financial, are obvious enough to companies whose main purpose is to show profits at the end of their fiscal year. Although the Government of Canada is not geared toward this goal of financial gains, it is supposed to work for gains in the well-being of its citizens.
One of the major problems facing the native people today is the high incidence of arrests for various reasons. The majority of these stem from a lack of purpose or frustration in achieving goals. This leads to family problems, school drop-outs, alcoholism, drug addiction and a high rate of suicides. One of the major methods of combating these problems is the sport and recreation programs which have been set up in many of the native communities across the country. The Band leaders have realized that these programs are of the utmost importance in helping to occupy the time of native citizens, and in providing them with a sense of purpose, a forum for expression and a means of self-improvement.
The staging of athletic events by the various native communities is beneficial not only in the training of athletes, but also for all those in related fields. Managers, coaches and game officials are trained and developed. Sporting sites are constructed with facilities which remain at the host site for future use by the host community. The other aspects involve security preparations and maintenance, the feeding and hous-
March 19, 1981

ing of outside participants and the preparation and operation of first aid and sanitation facilities. All these aspects, along with the very important fund-raising activities, may take up to two years prior to the actual events.
From all the details given above, it is clearly evident that such a program of sport and recreation within the native communities has far-reaching and long-lasting benefits, the most important being the improved mental and physical health of the native population. How is it possible then that the government can cancel such a program without any prior consultation with the native organizations about the results of such a cancellation?
It is time for the Government of Canada to accept its responsibilities with respect to the native population on a mature and proper level. Their treatment as responsible citizens of this country is long overdue. They can no longer be considered as some distant and unwanted relatives to be pushed around from one department to another in the hope that the resulting confusion will erase the mismanagement and lack of commitment to Canada's first citizens.
1 strongly urge the government to consider its decisions and to reinstate the very worth-while Indian sports and recreation program immediately. That program was devised and studied and would have been implemented had the Clark government still been in power.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT-TERMINATION OF NATIVE SPORT AND RECREATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the native sport and recreation program was initiated in 1972 for a Five-year experimental period. The program was subsequently extended on a year to year basis, and in the current year a total of $1,092,000 has been shared among some thirty-three Inuit, status Indian, and non-status and Metis associations across the country. These contributions enabled the associations to employ recreation co-ordinators and to implement modest programs of sport, fitness, physical recreation and leadership development.
The decision to terminate the program was taken only after consideration of several alternatives in consultation with many of the recipient groups and other government departments. The Fitness and Amateur Sport is a relatively small organization without an extensive network of field offices, and the programs, taking place as they did in many locations, were difficult to monitor and evaluate. The Fitness and Amateur Sport's mandate is limited to support of programs of sport and physical recreation, leading to increased levels of sport excellence and fitness. However, many of the groups served saw as their First priority projects that were more in the area of cultural and community development. Fitness and Amateur Sport lacks expertise in dealing with the special and somewhat unique needs of native people and, as a result, many frustrations and administrative problems were encountered.
Despite these problems however, the program also met with a measure of success at the local level, and I have no doubt that in the absence of any alternative it will be missed.
Adjournment Debate
An amount of money comparable to that provided this year has been placed in the social development envelope, and an exploration is currently taking place as to how it might best be administered so as to provide the most effective support for programs in the general field of health and an enhanced lifestyle for native people. Discussions are ensuing with other government departments in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to amplify some of the concerns I raised in a question on March 9 with respect to the future of the grain transportation authority in Winnipeg.
As some of us know, the Grain Transportation Authority has served a very valuable function in terms of increasing Canada's ability to export grain. We all know that we have unlimited capacity-or at least very large capacity-to produce grain. Our problem in the past number of years has been to get the grain, once it is produced, to the export position. This is why the Grain Transportation Authority was originally envisaged and set up by the previous government.
I point out, as I did in my question, that it took roughly five months from the time the previous government was elected until the terms of reference for the Grain Transportation Authority were established. This involved some elaborate and long negotiations. I see that my colleague, the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight), is in the House this evening. He was part of a group of members which took part in a study to bring about the formation of the Grain Transportation Authority. He, along with other hon. members, is well aware of some of the concerns and problems which were encountered in establishing the Grain Transportation Authority. It took roughly five months to get the Grain Transportation Authority guidelines negotiated with the Canadian Wheat Board and other parties concerned with grain transportation in western Canada. Once the guidelines were established a coordinator was appointed. That co-ordinator was Dr. Hugh Horner. I think his record speaks well of the choice made with respect to the grain transportation co-ordinator. It is a well recognized and applauded fact that in the crop year just concluded we increased exports of grain out of Canada by some 20 per cent, largely due to the catalyst that the Grain Transportation Authority provided to all parties involved with grain transportation in western Canada. In fact, not only did this appointment have the support of most of the industry in western Canada, it also had the support of some of the people who now sit on the government benches. I should like to quote the Minister of State for Trade (Mr. Lumley) when he appeared before the committee on transport. He said:
As you know, we heartily endorsed the appointment of Dr. Horner by the Minister of Transport and, as a matter of fact, we on this side would like to

March 19, 1981
Adjournment Debate
assist the minister in any way possible to give him back the kinds of legislative powers he thinks he needs to do the important job of moving grain in Canada.
Clearly the minister supported the concept of the Grain Transportation Authority.
The hon. member for La Prairie (Mr. Deniger), who is now a parliamentary secretary, also supported it. He said in the committee:
Among all the problems our grain exporters have had to face in Canada, there are the labour conflicts that have occurred either in the port of Montreal or in the port of Vancouver ... In your job description-
Here he was speaking to Dr. Horner.
-1 do not see where you are responsible or where you have authority in the case of labour disputes-
Clearly he also supported the concept of the Grain Transportation Authority, and clearly he was advocating that the authority be given some jurisdiction over labour disputes. So obviously we have had support for the concept of the Grain Transportation Authority from government members.
As I said in my question, the concern which I and many members have is that without a co-ordinator, effective performance in grain transportation is in jeopardy. We know we have limited amounts of facilities available to move grain. We hear criticisms continually from the government side that we in the opposition are speaking from both sides of our mouths. The government says that we in the opposition at one time advocate increases in government expenditures and at the same time show concern over rising deficits. Clearly this is not the case, and if the government were serious in some of the criticisms they level at the opposition it would appoint a grain transportation co-ordinator for the authority, because the job the authority did in the past crop year made very good use of the limited amount of transportation facilities we have in western Canada. This has helped to increase Canada's export of grain, thereby adding to our ability to earn foreign exchange, helping to maintain the value of our dollar, and generally assisting the whole economy of the country.
The Grain Transportation Authority is not an expensive operation, and the appointment of a co-ordinator is needed to see that it stays as functional and efficient as it has in the past.
Back in October, Dr. Horner resigned. At that time he recommended that his second in command, Doug Radke be appointed co-ordinator. The minister at that time said he intended to travel to Winnipeg within ten days to discuss with the grain industry whom he would appoint as a permanent replacement, and at that time he named Mr. Radke as interim co-ordinator. That is the situation today. What has happened in the interim five months-roughly the same time it took our government, of which I was proud to be a part, to set up the office of grain co-ordinator-is that this valuable tool in grain transportation in western Canada has been without a permanent co-ordinator.
It is no secret to those of us who are involved in grain transportation in western Canada that the morale of the officials of the authority has been low. Recently they lost one valuable member, namely, Bob Martinelli, and Jim Mantz has announced he will resign in June. The minister said in his
answer he was looking for that pearl to replace Dr. Horner so he could get the job done. I hope the parliamentary secretary will tonight announce some kind of time-frame in which a co-ordinator will be appointed, because if they delay much longer-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) informed the House on numerous occasions of his support for the continuation of the grain transportation coordinator's office.
With respect to the appointment of a new co-ordinator, I do not have to inform my hon. friend about the minister's interest in finding a respected and capable individual to fulfil this important role. The record speaks for itself. On the very day of the previous co-ordinator's resignation, the minister met personally with ten prominent members of the grain trade and spoke with several more by telephone for the sole purpose of determining their views respecting the role of the co-ordinator's office, desirable attributes of a successor, and any names which they could suggest.
In the interim, while a successor is being sought, Mr. Doug Radke has been named as acting co-ordinator and, I might add, has done a very respectable job. This year's experience in exporting grain has not been without its problems; with a labour dispute at Revelstoke last fall and flooding in the Vancouver area around the beginning of this year. Notwithstanding these difficulties, the various parties have shown admirable co-operation in the movement of grain. Exports to date this year are some 4 per cent to 5 per cent above the level a year earlier, a year in which a record was set.
This situation has allowed the Canadian Wheat Board to assure producers that they will be able to deliver all the wheat and barley they wish by the end of the crop year. The acting co-ordinator, the trade and, in particular, the railways deserve a great deal of credit for this situation.
That is not to say problems do not occur. Certain areas of the prairies have experienced congested elevators resulting from the slowdown at Revelstoke last fall and the fact that deliveries to Thunder Bay have not yet geared up for the new shipping season.
More recently, ship arrivals have been slow resulting in a backlog of cars to be unloaded. Empty cars are at a premium back in the country. This situation highlights the importance of having all available railway cars allocated by a central body so these cars can be allocated to those grains most urgently needed to meet export commitments.
In summary, the system is working well at the moment. The acting co-ordinator is doing an effective job. This provides the luxury of a little extra time for the Minister of Transport to find the best individual available for this important job.
March 19, 1981

subtopic: ENERGY-FORECAST OF REDUCTION IN CASH FLOWS OF OIL COMPANIES
ENERGY-FORECAST OF REDUCTION IN CASH FLOWS OF OIL COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in the adjournment debate this evening because of a question I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Laionde) on February 5, 1981.1 asked the minister if he agreed with the statement of Petro-Canada's vice-president of finance and planning, Mr. Joel Bell, as it was presented to the National Energy Board. Mr. Bell stated that cash flows of the oil companies this year would be reduced by 25 per cent from that of last year as a result of the government's National Energy Program. The minister answered my question by saying he had not read the statement, but that he would and get back to me.
That was six weeks ago, and I still have not heard from the minister of energy. I am quite confident that if I had not asked my question during the adjournment debate this evening, I would not have received a reply from the Minister of Energy. I hope I receive an adequate response from his parliamentary secretary.
The question deserves a reply because the vice-president of finance and planning for PetroCan said something very different than what the government indicated with respect to the effects of its National Energy Program. Specifically I refer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the supplementary question I directed to him with respect to Mr. Bell's statement.
Petro-Canada indicated that cash flows will be reduced by 25 per cent in 1981. I should like to quote from the brief presented to the National Energy Board as follows:
Cash flow available for reinvestment has been reduced by about 25 per cent in 1981 as a result of the fiscal measures contained in the National Energy Program.
Those were the words of Mr. Joel Bell of Petro-Canada.
The point to be made is that on January 22, the Minister of Finance said:
-despite the National Energy Program the cash flow to the industry as a whole is very substantial. It is growing, and when we add the incentive payments, growth in the cash flow to the industry in 1980 and 1981 will be very substantial indeed.
The Minister of Finance went on further and said:
-the cash flow of this industry in 1981, even without the incentive payments which are provided, will be 28 per cent higher than it was in 1979.
I repeat, "in 1979". Why the finance minister, this master of economics, chose to compare the percentages from two years ago-1979-is a secret that I await the answer to from the parliamentary secretary. On February 5, when I asked the minister a supplementary question, he said he stood by his statement. The government and Petro-Canada are saying two different things. Which statement is a reflection of government policy? How long does it take the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance to read the statement of Petro-Canada, made more than six weeks ago, before they can tell the country what is going on? Before they do read
Adjournment Debate
it, I would like to ask that the two ministers get their act together. I believe they are very confused. One thing is sure, the oil industry certainly is not confused. The cash flow is definitely declining. Petro-Canada admitted this when it purchased Petrofina. It asked the government to provide the $ 1.4 billion to purchase Petrofina. This was due to the government not having the money. Its cash flow had been reduced. The people of Canada were asked to purchase the equity in Petrofina, since there was no money under the government's National Energy Program.
There are other companies cutting back. Chevron announced a cutback of some $330 million in its exploration program. Mobil Oil is cutting back by $164 million-a reduction of 46 per cent. At least 60 per cent of United Canso's exploration budget will now be moved to the United States, even if Joel Bell of Petro-Canada does not underestimate the attractions of the U.S., where oil netbacks are three times what they are in Canada.
I invite both ministers to come to western Canada to see the drilling and service rigs heading south due to the lack of cash flow. These are miniature factories leaving Canada and taking jobs with them. Everyone but this government recognizes that the National Energy Program has not worked.
This is what the chairman and chief executive officer of the Royal Bank of Canada said about the National Energy Program:
We'll see more jobs lost, the Canadian dollar fall still further, the price we pay for imports increase. The notion that foreign ownership is bad ownership, and that we can penalize it retroactively, as contained in the federal government's National Energy Program, is living dangerously. It is damaging Canada's reputation abroad, and is fomenting wasteful bickering at home, just when we should be pulling together. It must be changed.
The chairman and chief executive officer of the Royal Bank of Canada made that statement on January 8, 1981.
But, how does this government react? It reacts in the same way whenever its policies are criticized. It bullies and it accuses the people making those statements of being disloyal. Out west the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that if the oil companies and the banks criticized him then he must be doing something right. This government confronts and bullies, but it still refuses to consult and co-operate. It must show some good will if we are to get this country moving again.
I ask the government to clear up this anomaly with respect to government statements on cash flow. I urge ministers, when they meet with the Alberta government next month, to walk in with good will and flexibility for the benefit of the entire country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-FORECAST OF REDUCTION IN CASH FLOWS OF OIL COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the National Energy Program was announced, some representatives of the petroleum industry have speculated as to what cash flows under the old regime would have been in 1981 and the years beyond. Then, without any apparent assessment of the benefits and incentives available under the National Energy Program, they simply concluded that the new regime would be less favourable to the petroleum industry.

Adjournment Debate
As set out in "The National Energy Program", the revenues available to the industry in 1981 will clearly be greater than in 1980. The program shows a 7 per cent increase in 1981 in estimated revenues in petroleum production. Since the announcement of the program, companies have indicated considerable interest in the petroleum incentives program, which will result in an increase in incentive funds made available to industry over and above those foreseen last October.
It now appears likely that revenues available to the industry from oil and gas production, having regard to increased incentive payments, will be in the order of 15 per cent above 1980 revenues. It is expected there will be new entrants into the industry, greater Canadianization, and increased exploration and development on Canada Lands. In total, these factors will result in increased benefits flowing to the oil and gas industry.
Mr. Speaker, since reference was made by the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight) to the statement of Petro-Canada to the National Energy Board in January, I would like to put on record what Mr. Bell then stated:
In 1981 our cash flow before income taxes will be reduced by approximately 12 per cent compared to our pre-NEP forecast-the main contributor to this reduction is the PGRT both on conventional production and on our share of Syncrude production. In terms of cash available for reinvestment after taking account of income taxes payable and before taking account of Petroleum Incentive Payments we anticipate a reduction of $115 million or 25 per cent from $470 million to $355 million.
That is the reference to the 25 per cent reduction in cash flow as referred to in the hon. member's previous statement. However, I shall quote further from Mr. Bell:
After Petroleum Incentive Payments, Petro-Canada's cash available for reinvestment in 1981 will increase by $103 million, from $470 million to $573 million; this is 22 per cent higher than our pre-NEP forecast compared to the 25 per cent reduction in cash available for reinvestment before consideration of PIP. Over the five-year period 1981-85, cash flow available for reinvestment before PIPs would be 13 per cent lower than our pre-NEP forecast but after PIPs would be 53 per cent higher.
